implementation_notes: kotlinx.serialization generates serializers for @Serializable classes at compile time (no reflection), so the mapper is Json.encodeToString/decodeFromString and a framework converter registers the column: a Room @ColumnTypeConverter on Android or an AttributeConverter on the JVM. Configuration is part of the contract - ignoreUnknownKeys buys forward compatibility and encodeDefaults decides whether defaulted fields appear in the payload.
pitfalls: Serialization is opt-in per type: a class missing @Serializable (or holding a lambda or platform object) fails at compile time or runtime, so the payload only covers what was annotated.
Json keeps ignoreUnknownKeys = false by default, which turns a removed field in an old payload into a read failure; keep the reader tolerant while the writer evolves.
In-place mutation of a nested collection inside the converted attribute is not seen by dirty checking unless the attribute is replaced as a whole.

variants.name: JVM Hibernate JSON mapping on a Kotlin class
variants.implementation_notes: On the JVM, Kotlin reuses the Java persistence machinery: Hibernate 6's @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) with a serializer bridge (Jackson's Kotlin module or kotlinx.serialization) maps the data class to a JSON/JSONB column, or a plain AttributeConverter keeps the graph portable across providers. Prefer this over a hand-rolled string column when the database must query the JSON.
pitfalls: Kotlin's default parameter values only reach the payload when the serializer is configured to encode defaults, so a payload written under another configuration can omit fields the reader expects.
Hibernate needs a no-argument constructor to materialize the entity; Kotlin classes with only a primary constructor require the no-arg/JPA compiler plugins.
